This is an audio note on sacrifice. You'll notice that the word sacrifice is in this passage. This involves killing an animal and offering it to a God. Basically, it's giving up something valuable to honor a deity. Normally in the Bible, sacrifices are made to Yahweh, but sometimes they're made to other gods as well.

If you wanna learn more about the biblical idea of sacrifice, look for our key concept story.

This is an audio note on the word Spain. In our translation, we use the word Spain to interpret the original Hebrew word "Tarshish." Most experts believe that Tarshish was a port city in the southern region of what would eventually become Spain. Some commentaries also point out that in a Hebrew understanding, this word would sometimes be used to communicate a great distance between things or something being as far away as imaginable. In our way of speaking, it might be a parallel to saying that it's on the "other side of the world."

This is an overview of the themes in Jonah. There are some themes in the story of Jonah that repeat a few times. The first one is people not responding the way you expect them to respond. Jonah is a messenger of God, he is called to obey God. He is an Israelite and would know God's law and know that he is called to obedience. Jonah should respond to God with faithfulness and obedience, but instead he runs away from God. The sailors, on the other hand, know nothing about God and have no understanding of his law. But they show concern for Jonah's life and try to save him, even risking their own lives. They only throw him overboard when they have no other options. In the same way, the people of Nineveh have no reason to listen to Jonah. He's no threat to them. He's from a tiny country that they're probably already making plans to conquer. They would have no reason to think Jonah's God had any power whatsoever. But all of the people of Nineveh respond to Jonah's message with repentance and a change of behavior. Another theme is a pattern where characters disobey God, receive a judgment from Him, then they repent, which means that they admit they're wrong and turn to Him, and then he shows his kindness in some way. This pattern shows up in the main characters of the story, which are the people of Nineveh and the prophet Jonah. These same themes, though, can be seen as lessons for the people of Israel. First. Let's look at Nineveh. Nineveh was a key city in the powerful nation of Assyria, but they weren't using their power well. They were violent and oppressive. They disobeyed God, so Godsent a judgment against them. He told Jonah to go tell them they were about to be destroyed. But very unexpectedly, they repent. They admit that they were wrong, and they stop doing all their violence and ask God not to destroy them. And he hears the request. And instead of God's judgment, they experience God's kindness. Second. Let's look at Jonah. Jonah was supposed to give a message to Nineveh, but he wouldn't do it. He disobeyed god. He got on a ship and headed the opposite direction. So God sent a judgment against him. He sent a strong storm that almost destroyed the ship, which would have killed everyone on board. And interestingly, the repentance and kindness are reversed for Jonah. God kindly saves Jonah from drowning by having a huge fish swallow him. And while he's inside the fish, he repents. He says things like, you snatched me from the jaws of death, and I will keep my vows. Third, let's look at the people of Israel and what they would have learned. Jonah did deliver the message, but when the people of Nineveh repented, Jonah was angry. God loved the people of Nineveh, but Jonah hated them. And this is the point of the whole story. The founder of the nation of Israel was Abraham, and God told them. The nation that came from him should be a blessing to all nations. But Jonah and the people of Israel had come to believe that they alone deserved God's blessing. Israel's calling as a nation was todo good things for other nations. But by the time of Jonah, they had disobeyed that calling. And like most nations of the world then and today, they only cared about themselves. They had disobeyed God's calling and now hated the people of other nations instead of showing them love. So we can see the disobedience and the the judgment parts of the pattern, but not the repent and God's kindness parts. This may be because the story of Jonah was God's way of challenging the nation to come back to their original calling of blessing the nations. He wanted them to repent, start loving other nations and receive his kindness once again

Well, Jonah hated this and he was furious. He said, "oh, Yahweh, I knew you would do this. This is what I said would happen when I was still at home. This is why I tried to run away to Spain, because I knew that you are kind and understanding and you don't get angry quickly and you really love people and don't want to destroy them. But if this is how it's going to be, just kill me. I'd rather be dead." And Yahweh said, "Jonah, does it make sense for you to be angry like this?" Well, after that, Jonah went outside of the city toward the east and made a shelter to sit under to watch and see what would happen to Nineveh. And while he was there, Yahweh, the Creator God, made a plant grow. And this plant grew up quickly and had big leaves to give Jonah some shade from the sun. And Jonah was very happy about this plant. But the next morning at dawn, God sent a worm that went and nibbled through the stem of the plant. And so, the plant withered up and died. And then God sent a hot wind blowing out of the east on Jonah. And so with the wind blowing on him and the sun beating down on his head, Jonah was miserable. And he said, "just put me out of my misery. Just let me die!" And God said, "Jonah, does it make sense for you to be angry about the plant dying?" And Jonah said, "yes, it does. I'm so angry, I just want to die." And Yahweh said, "you care so much about this plant dying, but you didn't make it grow, you didn't take care of it. It was here one day and gone the next. And if you care so much about a plant, shouldn't I care about the people of Nineveh? There's 120,000 of them, and that doesn't even count their animals. And these people do not know right from wrong. Shouldn't I care about them?"

This is an explanation on Jonah's plant. In chapter four, God teaches Jonah that it was wrong for him to hope for Nineveh's destruction by using a plant. God points out that the plant is to Jonah what Nineveh is to himself, that, just as Jonah takes pleasure in the plant and the plant brings him joy, Nineveh also brings God joy. God also stresses that the plant is just a temporary thing, that it's here today and gone tomorrow, which is as opposed to Nineveh, which has been there for thousands of years, which God planted and took care of for all this time. Finally, God points out that it doesn't make sense for Jonah to be so upset about a plant when Nineveh is a city that's full of people, people that God says don't even know right from wrong. And, since people are made in God's image, it makes sense for Jonah to care about these people and to try to teach them to come closer to God instead of hope for their destruction.

Well, after that, Yahweh spoke to Jonah again, and he said, "Jonah, get up and go to the great city of Nineveh, and give them my message." And this time, Jonah obeyed Yahweh, and he went to Nineveh. And Nineveh was a very important city in that part of the world, and it was huge. It would take somebody three days just to see the whole thing. And so when Jonah got there on the first day, he went into the city and he said, "40 days from now, Nineveh will be destroyed." And the people of Nineveh believed God's message that Jonah was speaking. And all of them, every single one, stopped eating and drinking and put on old ragged clothes to show how sorry they were. And eventually, Jonah's message reached the king of Nineveh. And when he heard it, he got down from his throne, he took off his royal robes, and he put on old ragged clothes, and then he sat down in the dirt. And after that, he and his officials sent a decree out to the people of Nineveh. And this is what it said: "people of Nineveh, you are hereby instructed to stop eating and drinking. And you are not to give any food or water to your animals. And you are to put on old, ragged clothes and to dress your animals the same way. And you are to stop all of your wicked and violent behavior and plead with God. Who knows? Maybe he will have compassion and not destroy us." And when God saw that the people of Nineveh had changed, he did have compassion on them, and he didn't bring the destruction that he had said he would bring.

attributes.transcription: This is a devotional thought on the story of Jonah. Now, Jonah is a story about God's mercy, and it's also a very satirical story, namely, Jonah, the main character, is a terrible example of a person who follows God, even though he's supposed to be one of God's messengers. He constantly disobeys God and argues with God and fights against God. And meanwhile, the other people in the story, the sailors and the Ninevites, neither of whom know God, they listen when God speaks to them. When God sends the storms, the sailors react accordingly. When the Ninevites are told they need to repent, they do so. And so this story fights against that idea that can crop up in religion that we have exclusive access to God's mercy or to God's love. Instead, God shows that he wants to love everyone. He wants to have mercy on everyone. And so when we listen to this story, it tells us that now that we have experienced God's mercy, now that he has shown mercy to us, now that he has shown love to us, we need to be people who help other people experience God's mercy. And if we don't, we end up looking as silly as Jonah does.

This is an audio note on the word gods. In the biblical understanding of the world, there are gods or powerful spiritual forces that rule over people and countries. These gods are subordinates to Yahweh, but he allows them to perform certain options for him. In written English translations, you could tell the difference between gods in this first sense and God himself, or Yahweh, by whether the first letter is capitalized or not. There's no clear way to communicate this difference in in an oral setting, but in our translation we try to make this as clear as possible by our word choices and by the context of the passage.

This is an audio note on the word Spain. In our translation, we use the word Spain to translate the original Hebrew word Tarshish. Most experts believe that Tarshish was a port city in the southern region in present day, Spain. An interesting detail of this word is that in a Hebrew understanding, Tarshish would sometimes be used to communicate a great distance between things or something being as far away as imaginable and our way of speaking, it might be a parallel to saying that something is on the other side of the world.

﻿This is an audio note on sacrifice. You'll notice that at the end of this chapter, the sailors make sacrifices to Yahweh. This means that they either killed an animal or they burnt grain or some kind of food. Basically, they gave up something that was valuable to them to honor Yahweh. If you want to learn more about the biblical idea of sacrifice, listen to our key concept story.

This is an audio note on death's door. You'll notice that, in our translation, Jonah says that he was at death door. Now, the original Hebrew word that Jonah used to talk about this place of death was Sheol. And Sheol, in the Hebrew understanding, was this underground place people would go after they died. Jonah references this idea again when he says that he was sinking to the bottom to be buried forever. In the original Hebrew, he speaks about being trapped at the roots of the mountains. Or even later on, when he says that he was saved from the jaws of death. In this case, the original Hebrew says that he was rescued from the pit. In each of these cases, Jonah is referencing Sheol. In our translation, we preferred these alternate phrasings because they communicated the same idea of being rescued from death without the requirement that one would have to have background knowledge of Hebrew culture and of the idea of Sheol.

attributes.transcription: This is an audio note on the name Yahweh. The most common name for God in the Hebrew Bible, using English letters, is YHWH. Many English versions of the Bible translate this name as the title "Lord." In our version, however, we've decided to pronounce this name Yahweh, and there's a few reasons for that. First, in certain contexts, it doesn't make sense to use the title Lord. An example of this could be found in Exodus, when God revealed his name. If you use the name Lord in this setting, then God would say, "my name is the Lord," but we know that "Lord" is a title, not a name. In addition, many of the alternatives that we've considered don't work for various reasons. For example, "Lord" is a very archaic uncommon word in English. "Master," another word that we considered, has negative connotations that we were trying to avoid. Now, we understand that some people find it offensive to pronounce this name out loud. This was not our intention at all. We think there are certain advantages to rendering God's name like this. For example, we think that using God's name could actually bring us closer to Him. We also acknowledge that this is the name God asked to be called by. It's the language he gave us to use when we talk about Him. If you want to learn more about the history of the name Yahweh, refer to our key concept story.

This is an audio note on the phrase "drawing straws." You'll notice that in our translation, we use the phrase drawing straws to describe what the sailors do aboard their ship to decide who on board was responsible for offending one of the gods. A literal translation of this Hebrew phrase would be "casting lots," and there are a lot of different views on what this actually entailed. Some commentators believe that the sailors threw a stone or stones that had some kind of marking on them, and the way they landed would indicate who is at fault. Others think that they threw bones and that the way the bones landed or were arranged provided that same information. In our translation, we considered two options to render this phrase. First, we considered "throwing dice," because this preserved the idea of a physical thing that was thrown, and that provides some kind of a signal or an indication. And this is closer to what the activity actually looked like. But in the end, we decided with drawing straws because this is much closer to the actual function of what they were doing, because drawing straws is the method we would use to identify a single person out of a group.

This is an audio note on the phrase, three days to see the whole thing. You'll notice that in our translation, we use the phrase three days to see the whole thing to describe the city of Nineveh and how large it was. The Hebrew phrase literally means a three days walk, and some commentators interpret this as saying that it would take three days to cross the city to go from one side to the other side.

While others think that it means that it would take three days to go through all of the parts of the city to see the whole thing. We preferred the second of these interpretations because in the next section when Jonah speaks to God, we learned that Nineveh is a city of 120,000 people, and any city of that size could be easily traversed in a day or even half a day in some cases.

It therefore makes much more sense to read this as saying that it would take three days to go through all of the different sections of the city and to see the whole thing.

Number one, because the primary function of prophets throughout the Bible is that of a messenger. They're someone who receives a special understanding or message from God and is then called to deliver it to other people.

Number two, outside of the Bible. The word prophet in English is almost always used to refer to people who predict the future. And so he tried to run away from Yawe. He went down to the port city of Joppa, and bought a ticket on a boat headed for Spain cuz he was trying to escape from Yawe. \v4 And so, as the ship was sailing along, Yawe started blasting it with a strong wind and a massive storm popped up outta nowhere. And the storm was so bad that the boat was about to be torn apart. \v5 And so the sailors started throwing stuff overboard to lighten the load. But nothing was helping against this storm. And meanwhile, Jonah was down in the cargo hold fast asleep. \v6 And so the captain of the ship went down to try to wake him up, and he said, "Man, get up. How can you sleep at a time like this? Call out to your god for help! Maybe he can rescue us." \v7 So... the sailors on the ship were assuming that somebody on board had offended one of the gods, and that's why this storm was attacking them. And so they had everybody draw straws to try to figure out who it was. And the short straw went to Jonah. \v8 And so they said, "What have you done? Who are you? Where are you from? What kind of job do you do? Why is this storm attacking us?" \v9 And Jonah said, "I am a Jew, and I serve Yawe, who is the God of heaven who made the land and the sea." \v10 When the sailors heard this, they were even more terrified, because Jonah had already told them at one point on the journey that he was running away from his god. \v11 But the storm was getting worse and worse, and so the sailors said, "Well what do we need to do to make this storm go away?" \v12 And Jonah said, "You need to throw me into the water. This storm is all my fault. And if you'll just throw me into the water, it'll go away." \v13 But the sailors didn't want to do that. And so they tried rowing to shore, rowing even harder. But it didn't work. \v14 And so then they spoke to Yawe and said, "Yawe, please don't hold us responsible for this man's death if it turns out that he's innocent. You are the one that sent this storm against him." \v15 And then they picked Jonah up and threw him into the water. \v1 So there was a man named Jonah, who was the son of Amittai, and he was a messenger for Eternal One. And one day Eternal One spoke to him and said, 
\v2 "Jonah, I want you to go to the city of Nineveh, and announce my judgement against them, because I have seen how evil they are.
\v3 But Jonah didn't want to do that. And so he tried to run away from Eternal One. He went down to the port city of Joppa, and bought a ticket on a boat headed the opposite direction to the city of Tarshish to try to escape from Eternal One.
\v4 And so, as the boat was sailing along, Eternal One started blasting the area with a strong wind and a big storm started raging against the boat. And it was so bad that the boat was starting to be torn apart. 
\v5 And the sailors were scared to death, and they started throwing some of the cargo overboard. And they were begging their gods to rescue them from the storm. But it wasn't working. And meanwhile, Jonah had gone down into the cargo hold and was taking a nap.
\v6 And the captain of the ship went down and woke Jonah up and said, "What is wrong with you, man? Get up and call to your God for help? Maybe he'll rescue us."
\v7 And so the sailors were assuming that somebody on board the ship had offended one of the gods, and that's why this storm was here (SHOULD BE THERE?). And so they had everybody draw straws to try to figure out who it was. And the short straw went to Jonah.
\v8 And they started peppering him with questions, "Who are you? Where are you from? What's your job? What have you done? Why is this storm attacking us?"
\v9 And Jonah said, "I am a Hebrew, and I serve Eternal One. He is the God of heaven, that made the land and the sea."
\v10 And when the sailors had heard this, they were even more scared, because Jonah had already told them at some point on the trip that he was running away from his god.
\v11 [missing: And the storm was getting worse and worse] And so they said, "Well what do we need to do to make the storm stop?"
\v12 And Jonah said, "You need to throw me overboard. This storm is all my fault. And if you'll just throw me overboard, it'll stop."
\v13 But the sailors didn't want to do that. And so they started rowing again harder to try to get to land, but it wasn't working. The storm was getting worse and worse.
\v14 And so THEY spoke to Eternal One and said, "Eternal One, please do not hold us responsible for this man's death if it turns out that he's innocent. You are the one that sent this storm against him for your own reasons." 
\v15 And then they grabbed Jonah and threw him overboard. And right away the storm stopped and the water was calm. 
\v16 And the sailors were were amazed at the Eternal One's power. And they made vows to serve him, and they even offered a sacrifice to him. 
\v17 And meanwhile, down in the water, Eternal One sent a huge fish to come and swallow Jonah whole. And Jonah was inside of the fish, alive, for three days.

This is an audio note on the word messenger. We use this word in our translation to interpret the original biblical concept of a prophet. First, we do this because the primary function of prophets throughout the Bible is that of a messenger, usually when someone receives a special understanding or message from God and is then called to deliver it to a person or a group of people. Second, in normal English context, the word prophet carries a heavy connotation of someone who's trying to predict the future, and while prophets sometimes do this, this by no means communicates their entire role within the Bible. Finally, we want to note that while the idea of a prophet doesn't actually occur explicitly in Jonah, we still refer to this idea because it's obvious that the text designates Jonah as a prophet. In chapter one, it says that the word of the Lord came to Jonah, and all throughout the Bible, this is a very common formula to show that someone is a prophet.

This is an audio note on the Hebrew concept of Sheel. You'll notice that in our translation, Jonah says that he was at death's door. Now, the original Hebrew word that Jonah used to talk about this place of death was Sheel. And Sheel. In the Hebrew understanding was this underground place where people would go after they died.

Now, Jonah references Shield and other places as well. When he says that he was sinking to the bottom where he'd be buried forever, he also says that he was saved from the jaws of death. In this case, the original Hebrew says that he was rescued from the pit. In each of these cases, Jonah is referencing shield.

Our translation, we preferred these alternate phrasings because they communicated the same idea of being rescued from death or a deathly place without the requirement that you would have to know about Hebrew culture and the idea of sheel.

This is an audio note on temple. In the middle of Jonah's poem, when he realizes that he's going to survive, he tells God, "now I know I will see your holy temple again." Jonah says this because in the Jewish understanding of God, God's presence is most concentrated in the temple, it's the point where heaven and Earth converge. So by saying this, Jonah is expressing his confidence that he's going to be able to return tohis homeland again and be in God's presence.

This is an audio note on the word Gods. In a biblical worldview, there are powerful spiritual beings that rule over countries, people, or areas of land, which they call Gods. These Gods are subordinate to Yahweh, but he allows them to perform certain functions for him. Although Yahweh is himself a God, since he's the most powerful of them all, and since he made them all, he's often just called God.

This is an audio note on the name Yahweh. The most common name for God in the Hebrew Bible is Yahweh. Since Hebrew doesn't write vowels, there is some disagreement on how to pronounce this name, but the general consensus is to pronounce it Yahweh, or more precisely Yahweh. Many English versions of the Bible translate this name as the title of the Lord.

In our version, however, we've decided to use the name Yahweh, and there's two reasons for this. Number one, this is the name God asked to be called by. It's the language he gave us to use when we talk about him. For example, in the burning bush story in Exodus three, when God revealed his name to Moses, he said, my name is Yahweh.

This is my name forever. It is what all future generations should call me. And number two, In certain contexts, it doesn't actually make sense to use the title of the Lord. For example, if you use the title of the Lord in Moses' Encounter with God that I just mentioned, then God would say, my name is the Lord, but since Lord is a title not a name, this doesn't make sense.

Now, we understand that some people find it offensive to pronounce this name out loud, but our intention was not to offend anyone. We chose this rendering because it's accurate and because we think there are advantages to rendering God's name like this, for example, we think that using God's name could actually bring us closer to him.

If you wanna learn more about the history of the name Yahweh, refer to our key concept story.

This is an audio note on the phrase "where I'd be buried forever." You'll notice that, in our translation, Jonah says "I was sinking to the bottom, where I'd be buried forever." This means that, according to our rendering, Jonah didn't actually die, he just came close to dying. You can also see this when we say that Jonah was at death's door, or that he was saved from the jaws of death, or in the Hebrew, that he cried for help in the depths of Sheol or was brought up from the pit. Some commentators believe that Jonah actually died, though. The Hebrew phrase doesn't have tenses here, which means that it could actually be translated viably as "I sunk to the bottom where I was buried forever."

This is an audio note on the morning practices of the people of Ninevah. In this passage, you'll notice that the people of Ninevah respond to Jonah's message by putting on old ragged clothes. Now, it's a very common practice in many cultures for people to show that they are mourning by what they wear.

For example, in the United States, people usually wear black when they go to a funeral. In Nineveh, however, the people put on something that's usually translated as sackcloth, and we've translated as old ragged clothes. The materials these clothes are made of, might've been something like a burlap sack. It would've been the roughest, cheapest, and least comfortable material they had available.

When they put these clothes on, it was a way of showing that they were humble, that their hearts were broken, and that they were in mourning. It might also surprise you that when the king gives the order to the people to do certain things, he includes the animals in that order. So not only were the people supposed to go without eating and drinking, but the animals were supposed to do that as well.

The idea was that when the entire community was threatened, then everyone in that community, including the animals, were supposed to respond in a way that showed that they were asking for forgiveness. And that they were sorry.

This is a cultural note on the mourning practices of the people of Nineveh. In the recording that you're about to hear, you might be surprised by the fact that when the people respond to Jonah's message, they put on old ragged clothes. Now, it's a very common practice in many cultures that when people are really sad or mourning that they put on different clothes. But the people of Nineveh, their practice was to put on something called that we usually translate as sackcloth, and we have translated it as old ragged clothes. The idea was that if you've ever seen a burlap sack, burlap is kind of that old rough material. This would have been the cheapest and least comfortable material that they had available. The idea seems to be that when they put these clothes on, it was a way of showing that they were humble, that their hearts were broken, and that they were mourning. It also might surprise you that when the king gives the order to the people to do certain things, he includes the animals in that order. So not only were the people supposed to fast, but the animals were to fast as well. And not only were the people to put on old ragged clothes, but they were to dress their animals that way as well. The idea seems to be that when the whole community was threatened, then the whole community, including the animals, were to respond in as how of sorrow, in a show of repentance. And so that seems to be why they dress their animals this way as well.

\v1 Now after that, Yawe spoke to Jonah again and said, \v2 “Get up and go to the great city of Nineveh and give them my message.” \v3 And this time Jonah obeyed Yawe, and he went to Nineveh. Now Nineveh was a very important city in the part of the world and it was huge. It would take somebody three days just to see the whole thing. \v4 And so, when Jonah got there, on the first day he went into the city and he said, "Forty days from now Nineveh will be destroyed!" \v5 And the people of Nineveh believed Jonah's message from God, and all of them, every single one of them, stopped eating and drinking and they put on old ragged clothes instead of their regular clothes, to show how sorry they were. \v6 Eventually, Jonah's message reached the king of Nineveh. And when he heard it, he got down from his throne, he took off his royal clothes and put on ragged clothes, and then he sat down in the dirt. \v7 And then he and his officials sent a message, an order, out to the people of Nineveh. And this is what it said: "People of Nineveh, you are hereby instructed to stop eating and drinking. \v8 You are not to give food or water to any of your animals. You are to put on ragged clothes, and dress your animals the same way. And you are to stop all of your evil and violent behavior. And call out to God. \v9 Who knows? Maybe he'll have compassion on us and we won't be destroyed. \v10 And when God saw that the people of Nineveh had changed, He did have compassion on them and he didn't destroy them.

Meanwhile, down in the water, Yahweh gave the command and a huge fish came and swallowed Jonah whole. And Jonah was inside of the fish for three days. And while he was in there, he spoke to Yahweh, his God. He said, "I thought I was dead. I thought I was done. But when I called out to you for help, you'd listen. And I was at death's door, but when I cried out to you, you heard me. You threw me into the water, into the middle of the sea. Your violent waves were crashing down on me. Your currents were dragging me under. You were done with me, or so I thought. Now I know I will see your temple again. I was drowning in the water. I was sinking into the deep. Seaweed was wrapped around my head. I was sinking to the bottom, where I'd be buried forever. But you, Yahweh, my God, you snatched me from the jaws of death. As my life was slipping away, I remembered you, Yahweh. I lifted my plea to you in your holy temple. The people who cling to empty worthless gods turn their backs on your love. But here's what I will do. I will offer sacrifices to you while I sing songs thanking you. And I will keep all of my vows because Yahweh is the only god who rescues." And then, Yahweh gave the command again and the fish spit Jonah out onto the shore.

This is an audio note on the phrase "three days to see the whole thing." You'll notice that, in our translation, we use the phrase "three days to see the whole thing" to describe the city of Nineveh and how large it was. The Hebrew phrase literally means "a three days walk" and some commentators interpret this as saying that it would take three days to cross the city, to go from one side to the other side, while others think that it means that it would take three days to go through all of the parts of the city, to see the whole thing. We preferred the second of these interpretations because in the next section, when Jonah speaks to God, we learned that Nineveh is a city of 120,000 people, and any city of that size could be easily traversed in a day or even half a day in some cases. It, therefore, makes much more sense to read this as saying that it would take three days to go through all of the different sections of the city and to see the whole thing.

attributes.transcription: So, there was a man named Jonah who was a messenger for Yahweh. He was the son of Amatai. And one day, Yahweh spoke to Jonah and said, "Jonah, get up and go to the great city of Nineveh and announce my judgment against them because I have seen the horrifyingly evil things that they do." But Jonah didn't want to do this, and so he tried to run away from Yahweh. He went down to the port city of Japa and bought a ticket on a boat that was headed for Spain, thinking he could escape from Yahweh, So as the boat was sailing along, Yahweh started blasting that area with a strong wind and this massive storm popped up out of nowhere. And the storm was so bad that the boat was about to be torn apart. And the sailors didn't know what to do. So they started throwing cargo overboard and calling out to their gods to rescue them, but nothing was helping. Meanwhile, Jonah had gone down into the cargo hold and was deep in sleep. And so, the captain of the ship went down to wake him up and said, "man, get up. Call out to your god for help. Maybe he'll rescue us." Now, the sailors were assuming that somebody onboard had offended one of the gods. And so they had everybody draw straws to see who it was. And the short straw went to Jonah. So the sailors looked at him and said, "what have you done? Who are you? Where are you from? What kind of job do you do? Why is this storm attacking us?" And Jonah said, "I am a Jew, and I serve Yahweh, the God of heaven who made the land and the sea." And when Jonah said this, the sailors were even more scared, because he had already told them at one point on the journey that he was running away from his God. And so, the storm, meanwhile, was building and getting worse and worse all around them. And so, they looked at Jonah and said, well, "what do we need to do to make this storm stop?" And Jonah said, "what you need to do is throw me overboard. This storm is all my fault, and if you'll just throw me into the water, it'll stop." The sailors did not want to do that. And so, they tried rowing to shore, rowing with everything they had in them, but it wasn't working. The storm was getting worse and worse. So they spoke to Yahweh and said, "Yahweh, please don't hold us responsible for this man's death. If it turns out that he's innocent, you are the one that has sent this storm against him." And then they grabbed Jonah and threw him overboard. And right away, the storm stopped and the water was calm. And when the sailors saw this, they were scared to death of Yahweh. And so, they made a sacrifice to him and made vows to him right then and there.

\v1 And Eternal One spoke to Jonah again and said, 

\v2 “Get up and go to the city of Nineveh and give them my message.”
\v3 And this time Jonah obeyed and he went to the city of Nineveh. Now Nineveh was a very important city in the region and it was very large. It would take three days to make your way all the way through the city. 

\v4 And on his first day Jonah went into the city and he proclaimed to the people, "In forty days Nineveh will be destroyed!" 

\v5 And the people of Nineveh believed God's message, and all of them stopped eating, every single one of them, and they put on ragged clothes to show how sorry they were.
\v6 And when the king of Nineveh heard Jonah’s message he got down from his throne, took off his royal clothes, he put on old ragged clothes, and he sat down in the dirt. 

\v7 And the king and his officials issued an order that said: "All the people of Nineveh and all of the animals will stop eating and drinking, 

\v8 and the people and the animals will put on old rags. And let everyone stop their evil and violent behavior. Let everyone cry out to God. 

\v9 And who knows? Maybe he will have compassion and not destroy us. 
\v10 And when God saw the change among the people, He did have compassion and he not to destroy them.

This is an overview of the themes in Jonah. There are some themes in the story of Jonah that repeat a few times. The first one is people not responding in the way that you would expect them to. Jonah is a messenger of Yahweh. He is called to obey him. He is an Israelite and would know God's instructions and know that he's called to obedience, but instead he runs away from God.

The sailors on the other hand, know nothing about Yahweh and have no understanding of his instructions, but they show concern for Jonah's life and try to save him even risking their own lives. They only throw him overboard when they have no other options. In the same way that people of Nineveh have no reason to listen to Jonah, he's no threat to them.

He comes from a tiny country that they're probably already making plans to conquer. They would have no reason to think that Jonah's God had any power over them whatsoever. But all the people of Nineveh respond to Jonah's message by changing their behavior and turning to God. Another theme is a recurring pattern where characters disobey God, receive judgment from him, reconcile with them, and then he shows them his kindness.

We concede this pattern with the people of Nineveh, with Jonah, and even with the people of Israel. First, let's look at Nineveh. Nineveh was a key city in the powerful nation of Assyria, but they weren't using their power well. They were violent and oppressive. They disobeyed God, so God sent a judgment against them.

He told Jonah to go to them and tell them that they were about to be destroyed. But very unexpectedly. They reconcile with God. They admit that they were wrong and they stopped being violent, and they asked God not to destroy them, and he heard their request and instead of God's judgment, they experienced his kindness.

Second, let's look at Jonah. Jonah was supposed to give a message to Nineveh, but he wouldn't do it. He disobeyed God. He got in a ship and headed in the opposite direction. So God sent a judgment against him. He sent a strong storm that almost completely destroyed the ship, which would've killed everyone on board.

And interestingly, the reconciliation and the kindness are reversed. In Jonah's case, God kindly saves Jonah from drowning by having a huge fish swallow him. And while he's inside the fish, he reconciles with God. He says things like, you snatched me from the jaws of death and I will keep my vows. Third, let's look at the people of Israel and what they would've learned.

Jonah did deliver the message, but when the people of Nineveh reconciled with God, Jonah was angry. God loved the people of Nineveh, but Jonah hated them, and this is the point of the entire story. The founder of the Nation of Israel was Abraham, and God told him that the nation that came from him should be kind to all other nations.

But Jonah and the people of Israel had come to believe that they alone deserved God's kindness. Israel's calling as a nation was to do good things for other nations, but by the time of Jonah, they had disobeyed this calling. Like most nations of the world back then, and even today, they only cared about themselves.

They disobeyed God's calling and now hated the people from other countries instead of showing them love. So we can see the disobedience and the judgment parts of the pattern, but not the reconciliation with God or his kindness. This may be because the story of Jonah was God's way of challenging the nation of Israel to come back to their original calling of showing kindness to other nations.

God wanted them to reconcile with him, start loving other nations and receive his kindness once again.
